entities.name: Julián Lobera y Valtierra
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Julián Lobera y Valtierra (died 1435-08-21) emerged as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in the Crown of Aragon during the tumultuous late Medieval period, notably as a steadfast supporter of Antipope Benedict XIII throughout the Western Schism. Born likely in Munébrega, Aragon, in the mid-14th century, his career exemplifies the profound intertwining of spiritual authority, regional power politics, and personal ambition that characterized the era. As Bishop of Tarazona from 1409 and later elevated to cardinal by Benedict XIII, Lobera y Valtierra wielded significant influence within the Aragonese court, navigating the complex diplomatic currents that sought to resolve the papal division while simultaneously safeguarding Aragonese interests.

Lobera y Valtierra's most defining role was his unwavering loyalty to Benedict XIII, even after the Council of Constance (1414–1418) declared the antipope schismatic and elected Pope Martin V. He served as a key advisor and diplomat for Benedict XIII during his retreat to Peñíscola, actively participating in negotiations and defending the legitimacy of the Avignon line. This dedication saw him excommunicated by the Roman papacy, yet it solidified his standing within the Aragonese faction that continued to recognize Benedict XIII until his death in 1423. Beyond his religious and political maneuvering, he was also a notable patron of arts and letters, fostering intellectual and cultural life within his diocese and courtly circles, reflecting the broader Renaissance humanism beginning to flourish in Iberia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Julián Lobera y Valtierra played a significant regional role in prolonging the Western Schism through his unwavering support for Antipope Benedict XIII, influencing Aragonese foreign policy and church-state relations during a critical period. His actions complicated the resolution of the schism and highlighted the enduring power of regional loyalties.
